title: Strong Moves, Tricky Lines! | French Defense, Adv. Nimzowitsch
openingName: French Defense: Advance Variation, Nimzowitsch (4.Nf3), queenside undermining

moves.spoken: The French, and the pawn to e5 sets up the Advance. What follows is the Nimzowitsch treatment — a dangerous line that teaches closed structures and positional chess as much as it wins games.
moves.teaches: The Nimzowitsch Advance is a positional weapon built around the e5-clamp.

moves.spoken: Instead of the automatic c3 to prop up the chain, slip through the cracks with the knight to f3 — develop as if nothing were wrong and let Black ruin the pawn chain by capturing on d4. It looks utterly counter-intuitive, and that's the point.
moves.teaches: Nf3 over c3: concede the d4-pawn's shelter for rapid development.

moves.spoken: The bishop's best square is d3, behind the pawn. The bishop to b5 is a paper tiger — Black just blocks with the bishop to d7 — whereas from d3 it eyes h7, so if Black castles kingside a Greek-gift sacrifice is always waiting.
moves.teaches: Post the bishop on d3 for the h7 diagonal and the Greek-gift, not on b5 where the pin is easily blocked.

moves.spoken: Black lunges with the pawn to c4, and the bishop simply steps back to e2. In a closed centre you can afford to move the same piece twice — and White has provoked c4, which relieves all the pressure on d4 and hands White a free hand on the queenside.
moves.teaches: In a closed position, provoking ...c4 releases the central tension and frees you to attack a wing.
moves.plans: Be2, then break the queenside chain.

moves.spoken: Now break the chain at its links: the pawn to b3 leans on c4, and the pawn to a4 will lean on b5. Classic pawn play — put pressure on both pawns at once and dismantle the structure without delay.
moves.teaches: Attack a pawn chain by pressuring its members with your own pawns, base first.
moves.plans: b3 and a4 to break c4/b5.

moves.spoken: The pawn to a4 hits b5, the base of the chain — and note the tactical detail: the defence ...a6 is futile, because after the trade on b5 Black can't recapture with the a-pawn without hanging the undefended rook on a8. Timing is everything; strike before Black consolidates.
moves.teaches: a4 undermines b5; ...a6 fails because ...axb5 drops the a8-rook — act before the defender arrives.
moves.plans: a4 now, exploit the loose rook.

moves.spoken: Take the base first — the capture on b5 removes the linchpin of the chain. Only then does the pawn on c4 fall, and with it comes a permanent structural weakness.
moves.teaches: Eliminate the base of a pawn chain before harvesting the pawns it supported.

moves.spoken: After the trades resolve on c4, White has achieved exactly the plan: a long-term, permanent weakness on the queenside. The c4-pawn is a chronic target that isn't going anywhere.
moves.teaches: Convert temporary pressure into a permanent structural weakness you can besiege at leisure.

moves.spoken: Castle first — it's safe, because Black has no way to get at the d4-pawn, and the knight on f3 guards e5 so a capture there is impossible. Then the pawn to c3 secures d4, and only after those preliminaries does White set about winning c4.
moves.teaches: Secure your own position (king safety, hold d4/e5) before going after the target.

moves.spoken: Black tries the pawn to f6 to open the centre — but that's counterproductive when you're behind in development, so welcome it. Capture on f6 and pry open the e-file, right onto the chronic weakness on e6.
moves.teaches: Welcome the opponent opening the centre when you're better developed — it exposes his weaknesses.
moves.plans: exf6, open the e-file onto e6.

moves.spoken: No need to force it — the controlled move is the rook to e1, keeping the queen back to guard d4 for now. With two weaknesses on e6 and c4 and no time to develop, Black simply cannot hold.
moves.teaches: With two weaknesses and a lead, apply pressure calmly — the second weakness does the work.

moves.spoken: The king came out to f7 to defend e6, but the knight to g5 forks it with check and knocks it back. The pawn is won — though there's still technique to show with the king this exposed.
moves.teaches: A knight check can fork the king off a defensive square and collect the target.

moves.spoken: Black's king walks into the pin, and the clinical punish is the rook takes e6 with check — but the check is just a bonus. The real point is that next comes the pawn to d5, winning the knight on c6 because its defender is pinned, and the whole queenside can stay home.
moves.teaches: Sacrifice to set up the follow-up: Rxe6+ then d5 wins the pinned knight.

moves.spoken: The pawn to d5 is the game-winner — it wins the pinned knight, and once that minor piece falls the king is hunted down. White won't even need most of the queenside pieces; the already-active ones are that powerful.
moves.teaches: Cash the pin: winning the key defender collapses the whole position.
moves.plans: d5, win the knight, mate the king.

moves.spoken: The finish is straightforward attacking chess: after the capture on c6 with check the knight defends the rook — that detail matters — and the king is dragged to c7. The bishop to f4 checks, and after the block the queen takes on d6 with checkmate.
moves.teaches: Bring even the sleeping pieces into a forced mating net once the king is stripped bare.

moves.spoken: The engine of the whole line, in Nimzowitsch's own conception: the e5-pawn is a clamp. It severs Black's position, cramps the pieces, prevents ...Bd6, and lets White pour development at the kingside — and the correct recapture on d4 is never with the knight, which would defeat the purpose, but with the bishop to d3 keeping the clamp.
moves.teaches: The e5 clamp-pawn is the point of the line; recapture on d4 with Bd3, never Nxd4.
moves.plans: Keep e5, develop, attack the king.
